title: Hybrid precision stitching: kernel contracts and runtime handoff
body:
Purpose:
This doc proposes a pragmatic runtime contract and lightweight kernel capability vector to enable 'stitching' across heterogeneous precision execution (INT8, FP8, GPTQ, AWQ, full-precision) within a single request. The goal: allow per-layer or per-block precision transitions without violating KV-cache coherence, correctness, or SLOs, and to make scheduling/fallback logic deterministic and auditable.

Scope:
- Serving runtime kernel handshake and capability declaration for CPU/GPU/accelerator kernels.
- Rules for transitioning between precisions mid-inference (stitch points).
- KV-cache tagging and migration semantics when underlying representation changes.
- Scheduling fallbacks and priority decisions when some nodes lack a given kernel.
- Determinism and testing checklist for cross-precision regressions.

Design principles / constraints:
- Minimal kerneI surface: kernels expose a small capability vector instead of complex ABI changes.
- Safe default: if a runtime cannot guarantee correctness for a stitch, prefer model-variant fallback rather than silent conversion.
- Preserve token-level determinism for identical inputs+model+seed across runs when using identical kernel capabilities.
- Low-latency handshake: kernel capability negotiation should add <250us on cold path and be cached for warm workers.

Key concepts (short names used later):
- Stitch point: a boundary in the model graph where execution precision may change (e.g., after an attention block or MLP).
- Kernel capability vector (KCV): small bitmap describing kernel features (bit flags).
- Representation token (rep-tag): tag attached to cached KV entries that identifies numeric format & provenance.
- Stitch adapter: runtime-managed conversion operator used only when explicit and safe.

Kernel capability vector (KCV) proposal (example bits):
- bit0: supports INT8 weight/activation path (symmetric/asymmetric)
- bit1: supports FP8 (e4m3/e5m2 variants) weight/activation
- bit2: supports GPTQ-style dequantized dropout-safe forward (reconstruction aware)
- bit3: supports AWQ-encoded inference path (packed blocks)
- bit4: supports KV cache read/write without on-the-fly dequant (i.e., store as native rep)
- bit5: supports deterministic rounding mode control (required for reproducibility)
- bit6: supports per-channel scales and transposed kernels (for certain GPTQ layouts)
- bit7: supports direct zero-copy mapping of packed weight pages (fast path)

KCV semantics:
- Kernels advertise a stable KCV string/identifier during startup. The runtime stores worker-KCV in the node metadata and uses it for routing.
- Comparison operations: KCV_A superset-of KCV_B means A can execute everything B can without conversion; equal KCVs are directly compatible.
- Partial overlap: requires explicit stitch adapters or model fallback. Runtime must log and surface conversions to ops.

Stitch point contract:
- A stitch is allowed only at an op boundary where:
  - The downstream kernel advertises a KCV that is either superset or has an allowed adapter.
  - The KV-cache rep-tag of keys produced upstream is readable by downstream (see KV rules).
- Allowed adapters are explicit, registered in runtime and implemented by kernels or runtime-only conversion primitives (e.g., dequant->FP16->quant).
- Adapters must be idempotent for a given source rep-tag -> target KCV transition to avoid accumulation of numerical error across repeated uses.

KV-cache tagging and migration semantics:
- Every KV cache entry carries a rep-tag: e.g., "INT8:per-tensor:scaleX:layer42:v1" or "AWQ:block32:v2".
- Read rule: a kernel that supports KV-cache read (KCV.bit4) can read an entry only if it recognizes the rep-tag or if there is a registered adapter from that rep-tag to the kernel's native rep.
- Write rule: when a kernel writes KV entries, it must specify the rep-tag to store. The runtime will record this on the request trace.
- Migration rule: an explicit migration job (background) can re-encode cache entries when a node pool upgrades (e.g., new AWQ-enabled nodes). Migration must preserve TTL and be visible in trace logs.
- Consistency: when multiple concurrent requests see a rep-tag change for the same key, runtime must ensure deterministic selection: use versioned rep-tags and last-writer wins with causal ordering preserved.

Scheduling and routing heuristics:
- Prefer exact KCV match for lower overhead. If exact match not available, prefer superset with no adapter.
- If only partial-match nodes exist, runtime computes estimated penalty = adapterCost + conversionLatency + potential numeric-risk-factor. If penalty exceeds request's latency budget, fallback to alternate model-variant (e.g., FP16 variant) or enqueue for capacity.
- Canaries & rollouts: new kernels (e.g., AWQ fast-path) should be rolled out via canary routing policy with percent traffic and safety checks for numerical drift.

Fallback policy examples (deterministic):
- Case A: model pinned to 'int8-fast' variant but worker pool lacks int8 KCV; fallback order: int8-capable superset -> adapter path (int8->fp16) -> FP16 model variant.
- Case B: KV entries exist in AWQ rep-tag but consuming node only understands GPTQ rep-tag: reject unless adapter registered and estimated error < threshold; log SRV-804 if rejected.

Determinism and reproducibility guidelines:
- Kernels that advertise deterministic rounding (bit5) must expose a control knob to set rounding mode; default must be 'runtime-deterministic'.
- Adapters that include stochastic elements (rare) must be explicitly flagged as non-deterministic; runtime will not use them for cached entries unless request opted-in.
- Unit tests must assert equality of token logits & final tokens for seed-fixed runs across common stitch scenarios. See testing checklist.

Testing checklist (minimal):
- Basic pipeline: INT8->FP8 stitch at attention boundary with small seed, compare token sequence vs FP16 baseline.
- KV-cache RTT: populate cache in INT8 rep-tag, route to AWQ worker via adapter; verify correctness and performance penalty < configured SLA.
- Fuzz transitions: random layer boundaries, random rep-tags, assert no silent hangs, no incorrect dequant shapes.
- Canary rollout: compare model outputs across traffic slices and run quality regression tests (evaluation prompts).

Observability / tracing requirements:
- Every request trace includes: initial model variant, per-stitch KCVs, rep-tags observed, any adapters used, adapter latency and numeric-warning flags.
- Alerts: numeric-drift rate per minute > threshold (configurable) must trigger regression alert and automated rollback to previous variant.

Open questions / unresolved tradeoffs (notes to self):
- How strict should rep-tag equality be for KV reads? We use versioned tags today but need a mechanism to allow forward-compatible tags (e.g., "AWQ:v* -> AWQ:vN" mapping).
- Adapter cost estimation: we need a small profiling harness to populate adapterCost numbers at build time and refresh in staging.
- Where to store rep-tag catalog? Lightweight key-value in control plane vs local worker cache. Need secure signing for rep-tag provenance.

Migration plan (high-level):
1) Implement KCV header and per-worker KCV exposure (hotpatchable).
2) Add rep-tag metadata on KV create/write operations and expose via trace.
3) Provide two adapters: INT8->FP16, AWQ->FP16 in runtime for experiments.
4) Canary AWQ nodepool with 5% traffic, evaluate drift on eval-set, raise to 25% if pass.
5) Add migration tooling for background KV re-encoding.

Appendix: quick examples (informal)
- Example KCV string: "KCV=0b01010111:v2" where bits map to features listed above; runtime compares bitmaps for compatibility.
- Rep-tag example: "rep=AWQ:block32:v3:pagehash=abcd1234". The pagehash ties to a weight page layout and is included in trace for forensics.

References / linked tasks:
- See GH:repo/runtime#1423 for the first KCV proto draft.
- JIRA SRV-804 tracks KV rep-tag and migration work.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally pragmatic and runtime-first: low-risk conversions only when explicit adapters exist. Please call out if any proposed default would cause surprise behavior to platform users (e.g., invisible silent conversions).
- Request feedback on the KCV bit assignments and if we should push to a compact hex string representation instead of binary bitmap.
